nutshell: Los Angeles (LA and Orange counties, 12.8M people) has no single folk scene. It is a sprawling federation of small ones, spread across a hundred suburbs, and most of its folk energy is in heritage dance and song rather than Anglo-Celtic tunes. By event count, the scene is dancers, not fiddlers. About 300 verified recurring meetings a month are led by international and Israeli folk dance (~95), Scottish country dance and céilí classes (~30), weekly heritage practice such as Obon, fandango, Danza Azteca and the Leimert Park drum circle (~50), and Songmakers' living-room hoots. There are about 23 Irish sessions a month (anchored by a 36-year-old Monday seisiún in a North Hollywood social club), about 35 bluegrass jams (many in Saturday-morning parks), only ~3 old-time jams and just four Saturday contras. LA's distinction is history and institution-building: Lummis's 1904 Californio cylinders, Western swing's naming, the Ash Grove, McCabe's, KPFK's FolkScene (since 1970), the Topanga Banjo-Fiddle Contest (1961), Folk Alliance (born in Malibu, 1989), and 18 NEA Heritage Fellows, from mariachi to Cambodian dance.

headline_stats.note: Counts are LA + Orange counties, in-person, inside the MSA. Online (Zoom) circles, Ventura County Songmakers circles and one undated Israeli session are listed but not counted. Seasonal heritage practice (Obon season, bon odori practice nights) is averaged over 12 months. Claremont items (Back Abbey session, Folk Music Center open mic, Israeli dancing) are in LA County and counted here, not for Riverside.

organizations.name: Songmakers
organizations.notes: The region's umbrella for home 'hoots': about 10 in-person circles a month in LA County, about 8 more in Ventura County, and 3 weekly Zoom circles. Incorporated as a non-profit in the 1960s, per its site. A search summary claims a c. 1953 workshop origin, unverified. Dues $10/yr per household. Reports more than $23,000 in assets and about $1,000/yr in donations to other music non-profits. Also runs an annual Roundup (election meeting, concert and jam; Feb 21 2026 in Woodland Hills), a Topanga festival tent with workshops, camping weekends (Kenney Grove, Fillmore), 'Music in the Mountains' (Nov, Camp de Benneville Pines), even group cruises. President Steven Berman.

organizations.name: Santa Monica Traditional Folk Music Club (SMTFMC)
organizations.notes: 48th year in 2026. Explicitly not a concert presenter ('we are a group of friends who come together to make music'). Former president Ross Altman. Sister club: Beach Cities Folk Music Club.

organizations.name: California Traditional Music Society (CTMS)
organizations.notes: Founded by Clark and Elaine Weissman after leaving Songmakers. Presented the Summer Solstice Folk Music, Dance & Storytelling Festival (a teaching festival), a New Year's camp at Camp Hess Kramer and a Center for Folk Music in Encino. Elaine died 2005, Clark 2021. Its domain ctmsfolkmusic.org no longer resolves (Oct 2026); current status unknown, probably inactive (low confidence).

organizations.name: Pasadena Folk Music Society (formerly Caltech Folk Music Society)
organizations.notes: Founded by Caltech graduate students Brian Toby and Simon Davies; renamed and made a 501(c)(3) in 2013. Keeps a 'Hear Here' regional concert list.

organizations.name: Los Angeles Sacred Harp (incl. Westside Shapenote)
organizations.notes: Three monthly singings; co-hosts the All-California Sacred Harp Convention when it is in LA (it alternates with the Bay Area). Announcements via Google group fasola-los-angeles-announcements and a public Facebook group.

organizations.name: Nevenka Folk Ensemble
organizations.kind: Eastern European / Balkan women's folk chorus (non-profit)
organizations.notes: LA-based women's chorus singing Albanian, Armenian, Bulgarian, Croatian, Georgian, Greek, Hungarian, Macedonian, Russian, Ukrainian, Ladino and Romani repertoire; women of all ages. 2025: concert and Balkan dance party at Culver City's Foshay Lodge (May 10); live music for the dance-theatre piece 'HALA' at LA Dance Project (Sep 5-6).

organizations.name: Topanga Banjo-Fiddle Contest & Folk Festival, Inc.
organizations.notes: Runs the May contest and festival; gives annual 'Music Legend' awards (e.g. Clark & Elaine Weissman 2004; Pitt Kinsolving posthumously 2016; Russ & Julie 2013).

organizations.name: Folk Music Center Museum
organizations.notes: Collection of rare instruments; the first pieces were a Stauffer guitar and theorbo from the 1880s, bought for $5. Presents the open mic. Dorothy Chase also began a Claremont Folk Song Society (date not given).

organizations.name: Ocean Institute
organizations.notes: Presents the annual Maritime (Tall Ships) Festival in Dana Point, Orange County.

organizations.name: Folk Alliance International (born in LA County)

organizations.name: Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann - Los Angeles (ComhaltasLA)
organizations.notes: Website claims weekly classes, rentals and sessions, but its Sessions, Lessons and Contact pages are unedited template text ('Edit this text to make it your own'). Branch name and activity level could not be verified; points to Facebook (ComhaltasLA). An AI search summary called it 'Ceol na nAingeal', which is not confirmed.

organizations.name: SoCal Uilleann Pipers Club
organizations.notes: Monthly meeting, 2nd Sundays 1pm at a private home in Orange County (FolkWorks recurring listing, last edited 2023; still generated into 2026). Active status not independently confirmed.

organizations.name: Scottish Fiddlers of Los Angeles
organizations.notes: 'Nearly 60 players' in 2026; 45 years old, so founded c.1981. Started by Colin Gordon, who introduced Scottish fiddle to the Topanga contest. Director Jan Tappan (joined 1981, director for 37 years). Repertoire now includes Cape Breton, Scandinavian, Welsh and some English music. Has worked with Alasdair Fraser, Natalie Haas, Ashley MacIsaac and Kevin Henderson. Monthly rehearsals and jams; annual spring concert; Oct 24, 2026 community concert at Pasadena Senior Center ($10).

organizations.name: California State Old Time Fiddlers Association, District 4
organizations.notes: Orange County district; monthly jam in Fullerton. The statewide association has 11 districts; its state contest is in Lodi (outside the metro).

organizations.name: California Bluegrass Association

organizations.name: Bluegrass Association of Southern California (BASC)
organizations.notes: Its website now redirects to a 'site does not exist' page. Its 4th-Sunday West Valley Music Center jam and 2nd-Sunday Vincenzo's (Newhall) Bluegrass Night have no 2024-26 evidence. Status unknown.

organizations.name: LA Bluegrass (labluegrass.com)
organizations.notes: Undated GoDaddy site listing about 9 LA/OC/Ventura jams; content post-dates Sept 2025.

organizations.name: Southern California Dulcimer Heritage (SCDH)
organizations.notes: Volunteer-run (President Barbara Gershman; P.O. box in Long Beach). Publishes a regional jam calendar, runs 'gatherings' (Costa Mesa, Oct 24, 2026) and a dulcimer rescue/consignment program. Support tiers $35-$250.

organizations.name: Klezmer Arts Institute of Los Angeles (KAILA)
organizations.notes: Gustavo Bulgach; weekly Zoom workshops; partners with SoCal Workers Circle and the California Institute for Yiddish Culture and Language.

festivals.name: Fiddling Frog contra dance weekend

festivals.name: Playford-to-the-Present Ball (first 'Los Angeles Playford Ball')
festivals.notes: First held Sept 29, 2001 at South Bay Masonic Center, El Segundo (Giovanni De Amici producer, James Hutson leader). 2026: Pasadena Scottish Rite, Renée Camus with Trio Con Brio, $50/$60, with a Friday review at Skandia Hall and a Sunday workshop.

archives.name: Lummis wax cylinder collection, Braun Research Library, Autry Museum (Southwest Museum)
archives.notes: Californio/Mexican American and Native American field recordings, 1904 onward, mostly made in LA. Counts: 450+ songs (Lummis), 450+ cylinders (KCET), 700+ including Native material (UCLA summary). Many are digitized via California Revealed and the Internet Archive (e.g. archive.org/details/WC.B.36, 'Laura', sung by Manuela Garcia). Transcriptions are in the Lummis Manuscript Collection's Spanish Song Series.

archives.name: UCLA Ethnomusicology Archive (World Music Center)
archives.notes: Holds UCLA Folk Festival 1963-64 tapes, among other things; individual sets are on Calisphere and the Internet Archive (calauem_000574, calauem_000588). Founding year not verified.

archives.name: John Edwards Memorial Foundation (JEMF), UCLA, 1962-1983, now the John Edwards Memorial Collection at UNC's Southern Folklife Collection
archives.notes: A core collection of commercial hillbilly, blues and old-time records. Published the JEMF Quarterly (ceased 1988, vol. 21). UNC bought it in 1983; it is the nucleus of the SFC (opened 1989).

archives.name: Southern Folklife Collection (UNC Chapel Hill): McCabe's Guitar Shop Collection, FolkScene Collection, D.K. Wilgus Papers
archives.notes: Takoma-era live masters from McCabe's, FolkScene tapes 1970-1997 (Odetta, Jean Ritchie, Merle Travis, Rose Maddox and others), and Wilgus's UCLA Folk Festival photographs and Irish field tapes. Much of LA's folk-revival sound archive now lives in North Carolina.

archives.name: Ed Pearl / Ash Grove Collection, Gerth Archives, CSU Dominguez Hills (SPC-2021-022)
archives.notes: 15 boxes / 12.5 linear feet plus audio and video (reel-to-reel, cassette, U-matic, VHS) of Ash Grove and KPFK material; strongest on the 1980s revival attempts and the 1996-97 pier club. Wikipedia says 'some 3,000 hours' of Ash Grove recordings survive; the finding aid gives no hour count.

archives.name: Woody Guthrie Center (Tulsa): Maxine Crissman 'Woody and Lefty Lou' Radio Show Collection
archives.notes: On-air songbooks from KFVD and XELO (fall 1937-mid 1938), fan mail statistics, and Woody's on-air banjo. LA radio history held outside LA.

archives.name: Library of Congress: Woody Guthrie 1940 recordings for Alan Lomax
archives.notes: Include 'Los Angeles New Year's Flood'. Recorded in Washington, D.C., not LA. LoC's WPA 'California Gold' collection (Sidney Robertson Cowell, 1938-40) is Northern California; LA items not verified (loc.gov returned 403).

timeline.event: Mission San Gabriel founded in Tongva country; the Spanish later called the Los Angeles Basin people Gabrieleno and Fernandeno after Missions San Gabriel and San Fernando. Precolonial Tongva lived in as many as 100 villages.
First African Methodist Episcopal Church founded in Biddy Mason's home: the root of LA's Black church song tradition.
Charles Fletcher Lummis walks from Cincinnati to Los Angeles (143 days) and becomes the LA Times' first city editor; the trip starts his fascination with Southwestern Hispanic and Native song.
Lummis founds the Southwest Society (western branch of the Archaeological Institute of America), which becomes the Southwest Museum in 1907.

Southwest Society buys an Edison recorder, horn and cylinders for $44.25 from H. C. Fiske Jr. & Co. of Los Angeles and begins recording Californio folksongs; Manuela C. Garcia of Los Angeles sings about 150 songs from memory (1904-05), the earliest group of recordings by one singer in LA history.
Lummis's article 'Catching Archaeology Alive' argues folksong recording is archaeology; composer Arthur Farwell transcribes songs (paid $50 for his first month, July-August 1905).
Azusa Street Revival launches Pentecostalism with ecstatic sung worship.
Lummis publishes Spanish Songs of Old California (14 songs, piano by Farwell), saying he had recorded more than 450 unpublished Spanish songs.
La Monica Ballroom opens on Santa Monica Pier (July 23); later home of Spade Cooley's TV show.
Artesia's Portuguese D.E.S. founded; the first Festa do Divino Espirito Santo is held.
From the 1930s mariachis gather for hire at 'La Boyle' (today's Mariachi Plaza), lodging at the Cummings Hotel.

KMPC station manager Glen Rice 'discovers' the Beverly Hill Billies, a publicity invention presented as rural folk from the hills above Beverly Hills; members included Leo Mannes (Zeke Manners), Stuart Hamblen and later Elton Britt. Jack and Woody Guthrie were hired to drive the costumed advertising wagons. The research brief said 1928; IWMA says 1930.

Leonard Slye (Roy Rogers), Bob Nolan and Tim Spencer form the Pioneer Trio in Los Angeles, soon the Sons of the Pioneers; Nolan had answered a 1931 LA Herald-Examiner ad for a 'yodeler for old-time act'.
First Nisei Week, with ondo dancing led by Japanese dance teachers.
New Year's Crescenta Valley flood (Dec 31 1933-Jan 1 1934) kills scores in La Crescenta-Montrose; Woody Guthrie later commemorates it in 'Los Angeles New Year's Flood'.

Woody Guthrie arrives in LA among Dust Bowl migrants (May); in July he and cousin Jack start on KFVD; Maxine 'Lefty Lou' Crissman replaces Jack and 'Woody and Lefty Lou' draws more listener mail than any KFVD show.
Woody and Lefty Lou briefly broadcast from XELO (Tijuana) before returning to KFVD.
After the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact, KFVD fires Guthrie and newscaster Ed Robbin; Guthrie's 'Woody Sez' column ran 174 times in People's World (May 1939-Jan 1940). He heads to New York.
Pasadena Folk Dance Co-op begins (its own 'since 1941').
First Southern California international folk dance clubs appear; members press homemade 78s when records are unobtainable (American Music Co. on S. Broadway sells some).

July 'battle of the bands' between Spade Cooley and Bob Wills at the Venice Pier Ballroom; Cooley's promoter Foreman Phillips makes the first documented use of the term 'Western swing' that year. Cooley's 18-month Venice Pier engagement drew several thousand dancers on Saturdays.
Cooley's 'Shame on You' (recorded Dec 1944) is No. 1 on the country charts for two months.
March 10: first Southern California folk dance festival at Griffith Park; 11 groups form the Southern Section. May 11: first Statewide Festival in Ojai, with 500 dancers and 3,000 spectators.
Within a year more than 30 folk and square groups are affiliated, including Filipino, Polish, Swedish and Mexican community groups.
Merle Travis, signed to Hollywood-based Capitol in 1946, records Folk Songs of the Hills ('Sixteen Tons', 'Dark as a Dungeon') at Capitol's request.
After the Soviet-backed takeover of Czechoslovakia, a motion to require loyalty oaths from member clubs fractures the Southern Section; it is defeated, but many clubs leave.
The Spade Cooley Show begins on KTLA from the Santa Monica (La Monica) Ballroom; it won local Emmys in 1952 and 1953.

Cliffie Stone's Hometown Jamboree starts (KXLA Pasadena radio, KLAC-TV), first at the American Legion Stadium in El Monte, later at the Harmony Park Ballroom in Anaheim; western-swing bandleader Hank Penny co-founds the Palomino in North Hollywood (c.1949-50).
Square dance clubs form their own association, starting the lasting split between 'squares and rounds' and international folk dance.

Bess Lomax Hawes moves to Los Angeles and teaches group guitar, banjo and folksong through UCLA Extension; Town Hall Party begins broadcasting from the Compton Town Hall (400 S. Long Beach Blvd, about 3,000 capacity) on KXLA and KFI/NBC, then KTTV television from 1953.
Bess Lomax Hawes moves to Los Angeles; she teaches mass guitar and folk-song classes (UCLA Extension, Idyllwild).
The White (LeBlanc) family moves from Maine to Burbank; brothers Roland, Clarence and Eric form the Country Boys, renamed the Kentucky Colonels in 1962 at Joe Maphis's suggestion.

The Unicorn opens on the Sunset Strip, the first folk coffeehouse in LA (Herb Cohen with Victor Maymudes per Maymudes; with Theodore Bikel per Bikel's biography; some sources say 1955). Cohen and partners then open Cosmo Alley. Doug Weston opens the Troubadour as a coffeehouse on La Cienega Boulevard.
Doug Weston opens the Troubadour as a 65-seat coffeehouse on La Cienega; its Monday Hoot becomes the audition stage of the West Coast folk revival.

Ed Pearl, a UCLA dropout from Boyle Heights, opens the Ash Grove at 8162 Melrose Ave in a converted furniture factory ($10,000 from friends and family; 250-seat hall, record store and folk-music school). First show: Guy Carawan, Brownie McGhee and Pearl's flamenco teacher. McCabe's Guitar Shop also opens (Gerald McCabe, Pico Blvd, Santa Monica).
Ed Pearl opens the Ash Grove on Melrose; McCabe's Guitar Shop opens; Folk Music Center opens in Claremont (Aug 12).
Riverside Rancho, the Silver Lake country-music showcase, shuts, pushing acts to the Palomino.
KPFK 90.7 signs on (April), later home of FolkScene.
The Ice House opens in Pasadena (Bob Stane co-owner 1961-1978); the Limeliters record Tonight: In Person at the Ash Grove on July 29.
Mariachi de Uclatlan forms at UCLA (formal course 1964).

First Topanga 'Banjo Pickers and Open Fiddling Contest' (Margot Slocum and Peg Benepe), about 500 fans; the Troubadour moves to 9081 Santa Monica Blvd; Town Hall Party's last show at Compton is January 14; Spade Cooley is convicted of murdering his wife.
First Topanga Banjo-Fiddle Contest (56th edition in 2016, 66th in 2026); the Troubadour moves to Santa Monica Blvd.

John Edwards Memorial Foundation formed in California (later housed at UCLA's Folklore and Mythology Center); D.K. Wilgus leaves Western Kentucky for UCLA; the Dillards move from Missouri to Los Angeles.

First UCLA Folk Festival (Wilgus), with the Kentucky Colonels, Dillards, New Lost City Ramblers, Pete Seeger and the Ashley-Watson band; Delbert Kauffman turns Huntington Beach's Golden Bear into a folk club; Bess Lomax Hawes starts teaching at San Fernando Valley State College (now CSUN); Ry Cooder, 16, debuts at the Ash Grove backing Jackie DeShannon.
Bess Lomax Hawes joins San Fernando Valley State College (CSUN); Ry Cooder's first public gig at the Ash Grove.
The Intersection folk dance coffeehouse opens on Alvarado St (moves to 2735 W. Temple St in Aug 1967); it later spawns many other coffeehouses.

Second UCLA Folk Festival; the Byrds form from folk singers meeting at the Troubadour; Scotty Stoneman joins the Kentucky Colonels; Bob Dylan plays a 'Golden Bear Presents' concert at Long Beach's Wilson High School (December).
December: Café Danssa opens on W. Pico Blvd, announced on the front of the LA Times Calendar section.

Rising Sons (Taj Mahal, Ry Cooder) form; Cafe Danssa, the international folk dance cafe, opens on W. Pico Blvd (December); the Kentucky Colonels disband after an October 31 show; Wilgus becomes founding chair of UCLA's Folklore and Mythology program.
The Chases open the Golden Ring folk cafe in Claremont (about five years; Rev. Gary Davis, Doc Watson, New Lost City Ramblers).
RSCDS Los Angeles Branch founded (inferred from its 60th anniversary in Nov 2026).
The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band forms in Long Beach out of jam sessions at McCabe's.
Alpine Village Oktoberfest begins in Torrance.
McCabe's first impromptu back-room show (1969 per Wikipedia).
Hadarim Folk Cafe opens at 1204 N. Fairfax (to 1975, then becomes Dance Arts Center).
Kinnara Taiko begins at Senshin Buddhist Temple after an Obon festival.

Byron Berline, out of the Army, joins Dillard & Clark and plays fiddle on the Rolling Stones' 'Country Honk'; McCabe's first concert is a benefit to get the stranded Elizabeth Cotten home (Wikipedia says 1969; McCabe's own site says 1968). After Altamont (December), LA County bans large outdoor events.
Veselo opens in downtown Anaheim, Orange County's own folk dance coffeehouse, sometimes open seven nights a week; Laguna Folk Dance Festival begins (per its 2020 50th anniversary).

Topanga contest exiled to UC Santa Barbara by the county ban (Peter Feldmann arranges it, then founds the Santa Barbara Old Time Fiddlers' Convention in 1972); Howard and Roz Larman start FolkScene on KPFK (February 3).
Howard and Roz Larman start FolkScene on KPFK after leaving Songmakers.
Wat Thai of Los Angeles established.
The Yom Kippur War undercuts Dassa's new venture Jericho; Café Danssa had already been sold to pay off its debts.
Self Help Graphics holds LA's first large Dia de los Muertos procession; Los Lobos forms.

The Ash Grove closes after the third fire in four years (patrons suspected arson tied to anti-Castro exiles); Clarence White is killed in Palmdale on July 15 after a New Kentucky Colonels show; Kevin Burke comes to LA to record with Arlo Guthrie.
Ash Grove closes after a series of fires (suspected arson).
RSCDS LA Van Nuys class moves to Valley College, where it still meets.
First LA Korean Festival.
Dec 31: Dave Blume and Carolyn Hester buy Café Danssa.
I Nyoman Wenten begins teaching gamelan at CalArts.
Folk singer Carolyn Hester and husband Dave Blume buy Cafe Danssa (December 31); the Blumes run it for 31 years.
Samoan Flag Day Los Angeles begins (inferred from its 50th in 2026).
Nevenka (Balkan women's chorus) founded; Folk Music Center Museum incorporated.
Bora and Marge Gajicki buy Veselo and rename it Veselo Selo.
Bess Lomax Hawes becomes the first director of the NEA's Folk and Traditional Arts Program, where she creates the National Heritage Fellowships (first awarded in 1982).
Bess Lomax Hawes becomes the first NEA Folk & Traditional Arts director and creates the National Heritage Fellowships.
Korean Classical Music & Dance Company founded by Don Kim.
California Traditional Music Society begins as a small amateur folk club (Clark and Elaine Weissman); Byron Berline records Live at McCabe's.
Santa Monica Traditional Folk Music Club founded (48th year in 2026).

First CTMS Solstice festival at Greystone Mansion, Beverly Hills (a 2010 CTMS mailing gives 1980 for the first festival and 'since 1981' for the series; Ross Altman says it began as The Dulcimer Festival).
Clark and Elaine Weissman leave Songmakers and found the California Traditional Music Society.

Colin Gordon founds the Scottish Fiddlers of Los Angeles after winning the first Scottish fiddle competition in Southern California (at Topanga); it calls itself the oldest strathspey and reel society in the US.
Carolyn Russell starts patio contras and house concerts in Garden Grove, the start of The Living Tradition.
Korean Resource Center founded (it later runs pungmul camps).
UNC Chapel Hill buys the John Edwards Memorial Collection, which leaves LA; CTMS incorporates.
Caltech Folk Music Society founded by grad students; Jean Ritchie receives CTMS's first Lifetime Achievement Award at CSUN.
Dec 31: The Intersection closes after 20 years.
Dana Point tall-ships festival begins (41st edition in 2025; year inferred).
An Claidheamh Soluis / Celtic Arts Center founded (date from secondary listing); its Monday-night seisiun has run for 'over 36 years'.
Gypsy Camp Ethnic Arts Center opens on Motor Ave after Mihai David's original Gypsy Camp café closes.
The Golden Bear closes (last show January 29) because of seismic retrofit costs and redevelopment; CTMS Solstice festival moves to CSUN (1986-90); Jan Tappan starts Fiddlers Crossing.
Golden Bear (Huntington Beach, OC) closes.
Approximate start of the Long Beach Bayou Festival (Cajun, zydeco, Creole), held at Rainbow Lagoon; it was in its 28th year in 2014.
First LA Guelaguetza, a small event at Normandie park.
First Fiesta de Santa Cecilia at Mariachi Plaza; the Leimert Park drum circle begins with Al 'Tootie' Heath; LA Classical Chinese Orchestra founded; NEA fellowship for jarocho Jose Gutierrez.
The Weissmans convene the first meeting of the North American Folk Music and Dance Alliance in Malibu; it is now Folk Alliance International.
The Weissmans convene 100+ organizers in Malibu: the founding of what becomes Folk Alliance International.
Mariachi USA debuts at the Hollywood Bowl; Nati Cano named NEA Heritage Fellow; Kayamanan Ng Lahi founded.
Topanga contest settles at Paramount Ranch near Agoura Hills after stints at UCLA (1971-72, 1977-85), Santa Monica College (1973-77) and El Camino College (1986-89).
Veselo Selo coffeehouse closes; its dancers continue as Veselo Selo Folk Dancers in Fullerton and Anaheim.
CTMS Solstice festival moves to the Soka University campus in Calabasas; it later advertised 5,000 attendees, 100 artists and 300 scheduled events.
Quetzal Flores discovers the Veracruz son jarocho revival, which seeds the East LA fandango movement.
The Palomino closes; Byron Berline moves to Guthrie, Oklahoma, and Gabe Witcher replaces him in Herb Pedersen's Laurel Canyon Ramblers.
Earliest All-California Sacred Harp Convention and Southern California Regional Singing found in fasola.org minutes.
Ed Pearl reopens the Ash Grove on the Santa Monica Pier; the city evicts it in 1997.
Giovanni De Amici starts a twice-monthly ECD series in Torrance.
CTMS cancels that year's Summer Solstice Festival to reorganize; Russ & Julie's house concerts begin (Oak Park, Ventura Co.).
Mariachi Plaza dedicated as a cultural center.
Bob Stane opens the Coffee Gallery Backstage, a 49-seat listening room in Altadena.
Bob Stane opens the 49-seat Coffee Gallery Backstage in Altadena.
The Living Tradition moves concerts, contras and jams to the Downtown Anaheim Community Center.
Paul Kulak creates Kulak's Woodshed in North Hollywood.
Hotel Cafe opens in Hollywood.
Sept 29: first Southern California Playford Ball, El Segundo.
FolkWorks print newspaper launches (January 2001-July 2007), then continues online with an LA folk calendar.
FolkWorks newspaper launched (15,000 copies bi-monthly).
Son del Centro (Santa Ana) and the Khmer Arts Academy (Long Beach) founded.
First Encuentro de Jaraneros de California (inferred).
Judee Pronovost starts Orange County ECD in Anaheim.
Las Cafeteras form at the Eastside Cafe; GAHFU (Garifuna) founded.
Culver City ECD begins (January); the Torrance ECD series ends; the ball becomes 'Playford-to-the-Present'.
February: Café Danssa closes after 41 years.
Cafe Danssa closes on February 3 after 41 years; Howard Larman dies and Roz Larman continues FolkScene.
Howard Larman dies; FolkWorks moves from print to online.
Los Cambalache founded; first Cambodia Town Parade (inferred); NEA fellowship for Sophiline Cheam Shapiro.
The Living Tradition drops its Bellflower and El Segundo Friday contras for financial reasons, keeping one Anaheim dance a month.
LA Old Time Social begins (inferred from the 15th edition in 2025).
Caltech Folk Music Society becomes the Pasadena Folk Music Society, a 501(c)(3).
October: Jan and Marc Rayman found Foothill International Folk Dancers to try new-dancer recruitment methods.
FandangObon presented at the Smithsonian Folklife Festival.
Roz Larman dies (Oct 10) after 46 years of FolkScene.
Last 'Los Angeles Regional Sacred Harp Singing' in fasola minutes; KCSN drops Bluegrass, Etc. after about 30 years.
The Woolsey Fire (November) burns much of Paramount Ranch; the Topanga contest later relocates to King Gillette Ranch, Calabasas (exact first year not found).
COVID: clubs move to Zoom, Fall Camp is postponed, Federation member clubs fall to 22. The Bobcat Fire damages access to Sturtevant Camp.
COVID cancels the Guelaguetza and most heritage festivals.
COVID: the Riskins retire from McCabe's and concerts stop (resuming in 2022 under Nora and Walt McGraw); the Topanga contest goes virtual.
COVID: Claremont Folk Festival put on hold (still on hold Oct 2026); Songmakers moves circles to Zoom (three weekly Zoom circles persist).
Ed Pearl dies of COVID-19 complications (February 7, aged 88); Clark Weissman dies (June); Byron Berline dies in Oklahoma City (July 10).
Collage opens in San Pedro (July); Clark Weissman dies (June 17).
Khmer Arts Academy closes; Anaheim designates Little Arabia.
Westwood Co-op merges with Tuesday Gypsies as Westside Folk Dancers; Veselo Selo closes Dec 31.
Alpine Village closes.
Coffee Gallery Backstage permanently closes (April) after Bob Stane, 86, is hospitalized.
Coffee Gallery Backstage closes (spring); the Whale & Ale pub closes (June), ending the San Pedro Shanty Sing.
Westside Folk Dancers closes; the Federation forms an Outreach Committee (Feb).
Phoenix Club reopens in Brea; June Kuramoto and Fabian Debora named NEA Heritage Fellows.

The California Dance Co-operative, now the Southern California Community Dance Coalition, brands its contras 'California Twirl'; the Camp Sturtevant weekend returns after Eaton Fire access repairs; the Celtic Arts Center adds a monthly extended céilí class (Feb).
ICE raids: the Guelaguetza and 20+ LA-area July 4th events are cancelled; first LA Gamelan Festival; Hanjuri Pungmul forms.

The Eaton (Altadena) and Palisades fires (January) hit folk-adjacent places; Topanga's Will Geer Theatricum Botanicum, where Woody Guthrie once lived in a cabin, survives and calls its season a 'Season of Resilience'.
Eaton Fire devastates Altadena (January); the shanty sing is revived monthly at Collage (May).
Narodni (Bellflower) goes dark 'until further notice' (July); RSCDS LA marks its 60th anniversary (Nov 28).
Gardena Buddhist Church's 100th Obon; Samoan Flag Day LA's 50th; the Guelaguetza returns; Farhang cancels Nowruz at UCLA; the 24th Encuentro de Jaraneros is postponed for rain.

Topanga Banjo-Fiddle Contest held at King Gillette Ranch (Sunday, May 17), with the 2027 date (May 16) already posted; the Celtic Arts Center still runs free Monday sessions at the Mayflower Club, North Hollywood; a Golden Bear revival is planned at OC Vibe, Anaheim, for late 2028.
All-California Sacred Harp Convention in LA (January); Songmakers starts a San Pedro circle; 66th Topanga festival (May 17); FolkWorks 25th-anniversary concert at McCabe's (Oct 11).

tunes_named_for_city.title: Los Angeles New Year's Flood
tunes_named_for_city.notes: About the 1933-34 Crescenta Valley flood; recorded for Alan Lomax in 1940. The only well-documented trad-style piece found that names LA itself.

surprises: By event count, LA's folk scene is dancers, not fiddlers. International and Israeli folk dance alone runs about 100 meetings a month, Scottish country dance about 27, and contra only 4 (all on Saturdays). There is no weeknight contra anywhere in a metro of 12.8 million.

The square-dance/folk-dance split was political. In 1948 Federation leaders moved to require loyalty oaths of member clubs. The motion failed, but by 1950 'all of the square dance clubs' had left to form their own association.

The Folk Dance Federation's memorial page lists about 640 former Southern California folk dance groups. 22 remain, many now meeting in senior centers in Chinese- and Taiwanese-American suburbs (Monterey Park, Alhambra, Cerritos) and inside the gated Laguna Woods retirement village.

One Songmakers hootenanny club, directly or indirectly, spawned KPFK's FolkScene (1970, after Howard Larman quit over a donation to a North Vietnamese orphanage), the California Traditional Music Society (1980, after the board voted out Clark Weissman) and, through the Weissmans, Folk Alliance International (Malibu, 1989).

Bess Lomax Hawes, who created the NEA National Heritage Fellowships, spent 1951-75 teaching Angelenos guitar in mass classes. She was Ed Pearl's guitar teacher before he opened the Ash Grove, and she MC'd the 1963 Topanga contest where teenage Richard Greene, David Lindley and Ry Cooder competed.

LA's longest-running Irish session (36+ years) is not in a pub. It meets Monday nights in a North Hollywood British social club, run by the Celtic Arts Center, which was founded in 1985 by James Connolly's grandson. Meanwhile about 15 pub sessions have died since 2002, one because 'Irish trad music has no place in an Irish pub'.
The Westside, home of McCabe's, now has no active Irish session. Trad has migrated to the Valley, the San Gabriel Valley, Long Beach and Orange County.
Bluegrass jams outnumber Irish sessions about 3:2 by meetings, and many are Saturday-morning park jams. The Long Beach one meets beside a dog park ('close your case, there are dogs around').

The phrase 'Western swing' was coined in LA (1942) by Spade Cooley's promoter, the year Cooley 'beat' Bob Wills in a battle of the bands at the Venice Pier Ballroom. LA's first famous hillbilly band, KMPC's Beverly Hill Billies (1930), was a radio publicity stunt.

Summer Obon is LA's biggest participatory folk-dance circuit: about 16 free bon odori from June to August 2026, open to anyone. Kinnara Taiko (1969) was born in an impromptu post-Obon jam at Senshin Buddhist Temple, on drums made from wine barrels. FandangObon puts son jarocho, bon odori and dabke in one circle.

Eighteen NEA National Heritage Fellows have lived in LA or Orange County, in mariachi, jarocho, Afro-Cuban batá (twice), Brazilian pandeiro, Persian santur, kunqu opera, Cambodian dance, kathak, Filipino rondalla, koto and more. Almost none are Anglo-Celtic.
LA once had perhaps the largest Louisiana Creole community outside Louisiana (~15,000), with church-hall zydeco dances, but no regular LA zydeco dance appears in 2026 listings.

LA's folk sound archive mostly lives in Chapel Hill, NC (JEMF, sold to UNC in 1983; McCabe's live masters; FolkScene tapes; D.K. Wilgus's papers). Lummis's 1904 Californio cylinders (Manuela García sang ~150 songs into a $44.25 Edison machine) stayed home at the Autry.

Altamont nearly killed the Topanga Banjo-Fiddle Contest. LA County's 1970 ban on large outdoor events sent it to UC Santa Barbara, spawning the Santa Barbara Old Time Fiddlers' Convention (1972). Topanga ran again on May 17, 2026 at King Gillette Ranch.
The composer of the contest standard 'Snowflake Breakdown', Wally Traugott, became a Capitol Records mastering engineer in the Hollywood tower, cutting Beatles and Pink Floyd lacquers.
A metro with the busiest US port complex has exactly one verified public sea-shanty sing (2nd Wednesdays, San Pedro), revived in 2025 by an arts space after its pub closed.
LA's song circles live in private living rooms: RSVP-only, capped at 15-20, potluck at 6 pm. Songmakers' center of gravity has drifted into Ventura County, outside the MSA.

The best listening rooms are inside instrument shops: McCabe's (1958; its first concert was a benefit to get a stranded Elizabeth Cotten home), the Fret House basement (open mic since 1969), Boulevard Music, and Claremont's Folk Music Center (bought by Ben Harper from his grandparents).

LA's old-time scene is entwined with animation: the Debs Park jam host is a retired Simpsons animator. An Illinois fiddler's tunes from Alonzo Janes, a once-enslaved Tennessee fiddler, came back to life via David Bragger and the LA Old Time Social.
AI search summaries were repeatedly, confidently wrong: they placed Madison's spelemannslag and Cincinnati's Riley School in LA and read 'Pasadena OR Long Beach' as Oregon.

data_quality_notes: Web search was heavily rate-limited across all threads (shared quota), and Facebook, Instagram and Meetup pages were mostly unreadable, so the census undercounts groups that organize only on social media or email lists, especially old-time jams, house concerts and heritage practice groups. The main contra organizer's website (California Twirl / SCCDC) was down all session; sources disagree whether the 1st and 3rd Saturday contras meet in Culver City or South Pasadena. Some dance listings show future dates (Nov-Dec 2026); these are recorded as last_evidence 2026-10 with next_listed_date. Modern square-dance club schedules come mostly from a Jan 2025 association listing (medium confidence). RSCDS Orange County class evidence is from May 2025. Scandinavian dance groups (Skandia South etc.) had no 2024-26 evidence and are not counted. Bon odori practice-night counts (~4.7 a month averaged) are estimates. Several heritage founding years were derived from edition numbers. Unverified: whether CTMS still exists (website gone), when its Summer Solstice festival last ran, current folk shows on KUCI/KCSN/KSPC, Songmakers' founding year, and Topanga attendance. Not found: Yiddish song circles, Georgian choirs, Black gospel quartet programs, a dedicated Irish music school, and an active LA zydeco dance series; these are 'not found', not 'absent'. The Traditional Tune Archive blocked automated access, so the tunes-named-for-LA result is medium confidence. Overlaps with Riverside: Claremont items (Back Abbey session, Folk Music Center, Israeli dance) and San Dimas's Huck Finn Jubilee are in LA County and counted here; the Riverside file lists them as outside_msa.
